questions.stem: Which energy source is non-renewable?
options: Wood grown in a managed plantation
Heat from hot rocks deep underground
Water stored behind a hydro dam
Uranium used in a nuclear reactor
questions.explanation: Uranium is mined from a finite store in the lithosphere and is not replaced on human time scales, so nuclear energy is non-renewable. Plantation wood, geothermal heat and hydro are renewable sources.

questions.stem: Why is biomass classed as a renewable energy source?
options: It is made only from plants that are native to the local area
It can be regrown on human time scales as fast as it is used
It releases no carbon dioxide when it is burnt in a power station
It is formed from fossil remains over millions of years underground
questions.explanation: A resource is renewable if it is replenished at least as fast as it is used, on human time scales. Burning biomass does release carbon dioxide; the argument for lower net emissions depends on regrowth absorbing it again.

questions.stem: Victoria's Latrobe Valley brown coal has a much higher moisture content than black coal. What is a consequence of this for electricity generation?
options: More electricity is produced per tonne, because steam forms more easily
More carbon dioxide is released for each unit of electricity generated
Less carbon dioxide is released, because the water absorbs it during burning
The coal cannot be burnt, so it is converted to natural gas before use
questions.explanation: Energy is used to evaporate the water in brown coal, so less useful energy is obtained per tonne and more carbon dioxide is released per unit of electricity. The water does not capture carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How is coal seam gas usually extracted?
options: Air is pumped into the coal seam so the coal burns underground and releases methane
Bacteria are injected into the coal seam to convert the coal to oil within a few days
Water is pumped out of the coal seam, lowering the pressure so methane is released
The coal seam is mined in an open pit and heated at the surface to drive off methane
questions.explanation: Methane in coal seams is held by water pressure. Pumping out the water lowers the pressure and releases the gas, sometimes aided by hydraulic fracturing. The large volume of often salty produced water is a key environmental issue.

questions.stem: Natural gas is often promoted as a 'transition fuel' between coal and renewables. What is the main reason?
options: It releases less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity than coal
It is a renewable source because gas fields refill within decades
It releases no greenhouse gases at any stage from well to burner
It has the highest efficiency of conversion of any energy source
questions.explanation: Burning natural gas releases less carbon dioxide per unit of energy than burning coal. It is still a fossil fuel, and leaks of methane during extraction and transport add to its greenhouse impact.

questions.stem: Which is a major environmental disadvantage of nuclear power?
options: Methane released when uranium is burnt to boil water for the turbines
Long-lived radioactive waste that must be isolated for thousands of years
Large carbon dioxide emissions from the fission reaction inside the reactor core
Output that varies with the weather, so it cannot supply base load
questions.explanation: Spent fuel remains hazardous for thousands of years and needs secure long-term storage. Fission itself releases no carbon dioxide, and nuclear plants supply steady base load. Uranium is not burnt; heat comes from fission.

questions.stem: Which energy conversion takes place in a solar photovoltaic panel?
options: Thermal energy to kinetic energy
Chemical energy to thermal energy
Kinetic energy to potential energy
Light energy to electrical energy
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electrical energy, with no turbine. Solar thermal systems are different: they collect heat, which may then drive a turbine.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares tidal energy with wind energy?
options: Tidal output is highly predictable, but suitable sites with large tidal ranges are few
Tidal output depends on daily weather, but suitable sites are found on every coastline
Tidal energy is non-renewable, because the tides will slow and stop within a century
Tidal energy produces carbon dioxide, because seawater is heated to drive the turbines
questions.explanation: Tides follow the Moon's predictable cycle, so tidal output can be forecast years ahead, unlike wind. Only a few locations have tidal ranges large enough to be economic.

questions.stem: A biofuel plant ferments sugarcane into ethanol. Which tension does this most clearly raise in terms of sustainability principles?
options: Fermentation releases radioactive waste, so the precautionary principle applies
Ethanol cannot be used in vehicles, so it fails efficiency of resource use
Land used for fuel crops may compete with food crops and natural habitat
Ethanol is a fossil fuel, so using it breaks the principle of intergenerational equity
questions.explanation: Growing fuel crops can displace food production or drive land clearing, which affects intragenerational equity and biodiversity. Ethanol from sugarcane is a renewable biofuel, not a fossil fuel, and it is widely blended into petrol.

questions.stem: Which renewable energy source uses heat from Earth's interior?
options: Hydro-electric
Geothermal
Tidal
Biomass
questions.explanation: Geothermal energy taps heat from hot rocks and fluids below Earth's surface. Tidal and hydro-electric energy come from moving water, and biomass stores solar energy captured by plants.

questions.stem: Which sequence of energy transformations takes place in a wind turbine?
options: Potential energy of the air → thermal energy in the generator → electrical energy
Kinetic energy of the wind → mechanical energy of the rotor → electrical energy
Thermal energy of the wind → chemical energy in the rotor → electrical energy
Light energy from the Sun → kinetic energy of the rotor → chemical energy
questions.explanation: Moving air turns the blades, and the rotating shaft drives a generator that produces electricity. No chemical or thermal stage is involved, unlike in a coal-fired power station.

questions.stem: How does burning fossil fuels alter the carbon cycle?
options: It creates new carbon atoms in the atmosphere that were not part of the carbon cycle
It moves carbon from the oceans to the lithosphere, lowering ocean carbon dioxide
It moves carbon from long-term stores in the lithosphere to the atmosphere far faster than natural processes
It moves carbon from the atmosphere into long-term stores in the lithosphere faster than natural processes
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels hold carbon removed from the atmosphere over millions of years. Burning them returns it within decades, faster than natural sinks can absorb it. Combustion does not create carbon; it moves carbon between stores.

questions.stem: About a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels is absorbed by the oceans. What is a consequence of this for marine ecosystems?
options: Seawater salinity falls, because carbon dioxide dilutes the dissolved salts in the ocean
Seawater becomes more acidic, making it harder for corals and shellfish to build carbonate shells
Seawater becomes more alkaline, causing carbonate shells to grow faster and thicker
Seawater oxygen rises, because dissolved carbon dioxide is converted to oxygen by water
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing the carbonate available to shell-building organisms. This is ocean acidification. The ocean becomes less alkaline, not more.

questions.stem: The concept of peak oil refers to the point at which:
options: the rate of global oil extraction reaches its maximum and then declines
the price of oil reaches its highest level in history and then stays there
all of the world's known oil reserves have been completely extracted
oil becomes the most widely used energy source in the world for the first time
questions.explanation: Peak oil is when the rate of extraction peaks, after which production declines as reserves become harder to reach. Oil remains in the ground after the peak; it is not the point of exhaustion.

questions.stem: A graph of global fossil fuel use from 1800 to 2000 rises slowly at first and then very steeply. Which pattern does this show?
options: A cyclical pattern of rising and falling use
A steady decline in use after an early peak
A non-linear increase in the rate of use over time
A linear increase at a constant rate across the two centuries
questions.explanation: A curve that steepens over time shows a rate of use that is itself increasing, which is a non-linear pattern. A linear increase would appear as a straight line with constant slope.

questions.stem: A wind turbine receives 2.0 MJ of kinetic energy from the wind and produces 0.80 MJ of electrical energy. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ energy in × 100 = 0.80 ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 40%. Dividing the input by the output gives 250%, which is impossible because no device puts out more energy than it receives.

questions.stem: A power station converts 1000 MJ of chemical energy in coal into 350 MJ of electrical energy. How much energy is not converted to electricity, and in what form is most of it lost?
options: 650 MJ, mostly as thermal energy
650 MJ, mostly as kinetic energy
350 MJ, mostly as thermal energy
1350 MJ, mostly as thermal energy
questions.explanation: By the first law, energy is conserved, so 1000 − 350 = 650 MJ is not converted to electricity. Most is lost as heat, mainly in the cooling water and flue gases, as the second law predicts.

questions.stem: In a coal-fired power station, the boiler is 90% efficient, the turbine 45% and the generator 95%. What is the overall efficiency?
questions.explanation: Overall efficiency is the product of the step efficiencies: 0.90 × 0.45 × 0.95 ≈ 0.38, or about 38%. Averaging the three values gives 77%, a common error. The overall efficiency must be lower than the least efficient step.

questions.stem: Water of mass 2000 kg falls 50 m through a hydro turbine. Using Ep = mgh with g = 9.8 m/s², how much gravitational potential energy is released?
options: 98 kJ
100 kJ
980 kJ
questions.explanation: Ep = mgh = 2000 × 9.8 × 50 = 980 000 J = 980 kJ. Leaving out g gives 100 kJ, and slipping a power of ten gives 98 or 9800 kJ, so check units at each step.

questions.stem: Water releases 980 kJ of potential energy through a hydro-electric system that is 85% efficient. How much electrical energy is produced?
options: 147 kJ
895 kJ
833 kJ
questions.explanation: Useful output = efficiency × input = 0.85 × 980 = 833 kJ. Dividing by 0.85 gives 1153 kJ, which is more than the input and so impossible, and 147 kJ is the energy lost rather than the energy produced.

questions.stem: Electricity from a power station that is 35% efficient travels through transmission lines that are 90% efficient to a kettle that is 95% efficient. A gas cooktop is 40% efficient. Comparing overall efficiency from the primary fuel, which is correct?
options: The kettle system is about 95% efficient, so it uses the fuel far more efficiently than gas
The kettle system is about 73% efficient, so it uses the fuel more efficiently than gas
The kettle system is about 35% efficient, so both use the fuel equally efficiently
The kettle system is about 30% efficient, so the gas cooktop uses the fuel more efficiently
questions.explanation: Overall efficiency = 0.35 × 0.90 × 0.95 ≈ 0.30, or 30%, which is less than 40%. Quoting only the kettle's 95% ignores the large losses at the power station, a common error when comparing appliances.

questions.stem: An incandescent globe converts 10% of its electrical energy into light, and an LED globe converts 40%. For the same light output, how does the LED's electricity use compare?
options: It uses 40% less electricity
It uses 4 times more electricity
It uses 75% less electricity
It uses 30% less electricity
questions.explanation: For a light output L, the incandescent globe needs L ÷ 0.10 = 10L and the LED needs L ÷ 0.40 = 2.5L, so the LED uses a quarter as much, 75% less. Subtracting the percentages gives 30%, which is not how efficiencies compare.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg mass of air passes through a wind turbine at 10 m/s. Using Ek = ½mv², how much kinetic energy does the air carry?
options: 100 kJ
5 kJ
10 kJ
50 kJ
questions.explanation: Ek = ½ × 1000 × 10² = ½ × 1000 × 100 = 50 000 J = 50 kJ. Forgetting the ½ gives 100 kJ, and forgetting to square the speed gives 5 kJ.

questions.stem: The first law of thermodynamics states that:
options: in every energy conversion some energy is destroyed and can never be recovered
energy flows naturally from colder objects to hotter objects without any input
a perfectly designed machine can convert all of its energy input into useful work
energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another
questions.explanation: The first law is the law of conservation of energy. Energy that is not useful is still present, usually as dispersed heat, so it is not destroyed. The impossibility of 100% efficient conversion comes from the second law.

questions.stem: Which statement reflects the second law of thermodynamics as it applies to energy choices?
options: Every conversion creates a small amount of new energy, so each extra step raises overall efficiency
Every conversion destroys some energy completely, so the total amount of energy in the universe steadily decreases
Every conversion is fully reversible, so energy lost as heat can always be recovered as electricity
Every conversion disperses some energy as unusable heat, so each extra step lowers overall efficiency
questions.explanation: The second law means no conversion is 100% efficient, because some energy is always dispersed as low-grade heat. The total energy is still conserved under the first law; it is the useful portion that falls.

questions.stem: A factory uses the waste heat from its gas-fired generator to heat water for its processes, rather than releasing it to the air. How does this relate to the laws of thermodynamics?
options: It breaks the first law, because the same energy is counted twice: once as electricity, once as heat
It breaks the second law, because heat is converted back into chemical energy in the gas
It shows the first law does not apply, because the factory now produces more energy than it consumes
It cannot beat the second law's losses, but it puts more of the dispersed heat to use, raising overall efficiency
questions.explanation: Cogeneration, or waste heat re-use, uses heat that would otherwise be dispersed, so more of the input does useful work. Total energy is still conserved and losses still occur, so neither law is broken.

questions.stem: Wind farm developers must monitor bird and bat deaths and shut down turbines at key times if deaths exceed a set limit. Which sustainability principle is being applied most directly?
options: Intragenerational equity, by sharing the wind farm's profits with local residents
Efficiency of resource use, by producing more electricity from each turbine
Conservation of biodiversity and ecological integrity, by limiting harm to wildlife
User pays principle, by charging the operator a fee for each bird or bat killed
questions.explanation: Limiting harm to birds and bats protects biodiversity at the site. Shutting turbines down actually reduces the electricity produced, so the condition is not about efficiency, and no fee or profit-sharing is involved.

questions.stem: A government levies a charge on each tonne of coal mined, and the money funds rehabilitation of the mine once it closes. Which principle is applied?
options: Precautionary principle
Intragenerational equity
Efficiency of resource use
User pays principle
questions.explanation: Those who extract and use the resource pay for the costs it creates, such as rehabilitation, rather than the community paying. The precautionary principle concerns uncertain risks of harm, which is not the focus here.

questions.stem: A government plans to burn all accessible coal now so that every household today, including low-income families, has cheap power. This would leave future generations with a hotter climate and no coal. Which two sustainability principles are most clearly in tension?
options: Efficiency of resource use and the user pays principle
Precautionary principle and efficiency of resource use
Intragenerational equity and intergenerational equity
User pays principle and the precautionary principle
questions.explanation: Making power affordable for every household now, including low-income families, serves intragenerational equity, fairness within the current generation. Depleting a finite resource and warming the climate harms future generations, which conflicts with intergenerational equity.

questions.stem: A company proposes hydraulic fracturing near a farming district, but the risks to groundwater are poorly understood. A moratorium is imposed until studies show harm would be minimal. Which principle does this apply?
options: Precautionary principle
Intergenerational equity
User pays principle
Efficiency of resource use
questions.explanation: The precautionary principle applies where the risk of serious harm is high but the evidence is uncertain, and it requires proof of minimal harm before proceeding. Protecting groundwater benefits future generations too, but the defining feature is acting under uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which is a biological process used to rehabilitate a former mine site?
options: Ripping compacted soil with heavy machinery
Building rock-lined drains to carry away runoff
Planting local native species grown from local seed
Reshaping the overburden into stable, gentle slopes
questions.explanation: Revegetation with local species is a biological process. Reshaping slopes, ripping soil and building drains are mechanical processes, which usually come first to make the site stable.

questions.stem: Why is topsoil stripped and stockpiled before mining begins, then spread back over the site afterwards?
options: It contains the seed bank, organic matter and soil organisms needed for vegetation to re-establish
It contains the coal or ore, which can be extracted more cheaply later once the stockpile has dried out
It is too heavy to leave in place, so it must be moved to stop the open pit collapsing
It contains salts that must be leached out before the mine's pit lake can be filled
questions.explanation: Topsoil holds most of a site's nutrients, organic matter, microorganisms and native seed, which speed biological recovery. Subsoil and overburden lack these, so plants establish poorly without returned topsoil.

questions.stem: Five years after rehabilitation, a former coal mine is covered in planted eucalypts, but monitoring shows few native ground plants, no fungal networks and few soil invertebrates. What does this indicate?
options: The site cannot recover, because coal mining permanently removes the possibility of soil life
Plant cover has returned, but soil biological processes and ecological integrity have not yet recovered
The rehabilitation is complete, because tree cover is the only measure of a rehabilitated site
The mechanical processes failed, because the site should have been left unshaped to recover alone
questions.explanation: Successful rehabilitation restores ecosystem function, not just tree cover. Soil organisms and fungal networks drive nutrient cycling, so their absence shows recovery is incomplete. Further biological work, such as adding inoculated soil, may help.

questions.stem: Base load is:
options: the minimum level of electricity demand that must be met continuously
the highest level of electricity demand reached on the hottest day of the year
the electricity generated by renewable sources during the daytime
the electricity used by a single household over one full year
questions.explanation: Base load is the minimum continuous demand across the day and night. Peak load is the highest demand, often on hot summer evenings when air conditioners run.

questions.stem: Which generators are best suited to meeting short periods of peak load?
options: Rooftop solar panels whose output peaks around midday
Open-cycle gas turbines and hydro-electric plants that can start within minutes
Brown coal power stations that take many hours to reach full output
Nuclear reactors that run most efficiently at constant output
questions.explanation: Peak demand rises and falls quickly, so it suits generators that can start and ramp up fast, such as gas turbines and hydro. Coal and nuclear plants are slow to adjust and suit steady base load.

questions.stem: Household electricity demand peaks in the early evening, while rooftop solar output peaks around midday. Which option best allows solar to help meet the evening peak?
options: Facing all panels west so that they produce their highest output after sunset
Switching off the panels at midday so that they last longer for evening use
Storing midday solar energy in batteries or pumped hydro for release in the evening
Installing more rooftop panels so that output in the evening rises to match household demand
questions.explanation: Storage shifts energy from when it is generated to when it is needed. Extra panels or west-facing panels can extend late-afternoon output but cannot generate after dark.

questions.stem: Which is a way an individual household can reduce its contribution to peak load?
options: Replacing a gas heater with a larger electric heater that runs in the early evening hours
Charging an electric car each day as soon as it arrives home after work
Running the air conditioner at a lower temperature on hot summer evenings
Running the dishwasher and washing machine late at night instead of early evening
questions.explanation: Shifting the use of appliances away from peak times lowers demand during the peak, a form of demand management. Charging a car or running heaters and air conditioners harder in the early evening adds to the peak.

questions.stem: Replacing an old electric hot water system with a heat pump that delivers the same hot water using a third of the electricity is an example of:
options: reducing personal energy consumption by using less hot water
improving resource efficiency by recycling the hot water
increasing the efficiency of energy conversion devices
replacing fossil fuels with non-fossil fuel energy sources
questions.explanation: The heat pump delivers the same service with less energy input, so the conversion device is more efficient. The household's hot water use has not changed, so this is not a reduction in personal consumption.

questions.stem: A household installs ceiling insulation and switches off appliances at the wall when not in use. These actions mainly illustrate:
options: reducing personal energy consumption and improving resource efficiency
replacing fossil fuels with non-fossil fuel energy sources
increasing base load supply from renewable sources
rehabilitating sites from which energy has been sourced
questions.explanation: Insulation reduces the energy needed for heating and cooling, and switching off appliances avoids standby use. Neither action changes the source of the energy supplied.

questions.stem: A region plans to close a coal-fired power station. Unions fear job losses, residents welcome cleaner air, a retailer warns of higher prices, and engineers say new transmission lines are needed for wind farms. Which statement best describes the decision?
options: The decision is purely technical, so only the engineers' advice on transmission is relevant
The decision is purely economic, so only the retailer's warning about prices is relevant
The decision is settled by the science, so the views of residents and unions do not apply
Stakeholder values, priorities and the need for new technology are interconnected and in tension
questions.explanation: Building a sustainable energy future involves interconnections and tensions between stakeholder values, knowledge and priorities, regulatory frameworks, data and new technologies. Decisions rest on economic, sociocultural and political factors as well as science.

questions.stem: Which option for a sustainable energy future most directly reduces greenhouse emissions from electricity generation while keeping supply reliable?
options: Replacing coal generation with wind and solar, backed by storage and interconnectors
Replacing old coal generation with new brown coal power stations of the same basic design
Replacing storage and interconnectors with extra rooftop solar panels only
Replacing gas peaking plants with coal plants that take hours to start up
questions.explanation: Non-fossil sources cut emissions, and storage plus interconnection between regions manage the variability of wind and solar. Rooftop solar alone cannot supply power at night, so reliability would suffer without storage.
